runs.name: plain-1
runs.topic: Splitting AI work into clear roles makes it safer and easier to audit and improve than one prompt doing it all

turns.content: When one prompt does everything (research, reasoning, drafting, fact-checking, and deciding), its failures are tangled together and nearly impossible to diagnose. If the final output is wrong, was the retrieval bad, the reasoning flawed, or the safety check skipped? Splitting the work into clear roles, such as a retriever, a drafter, a critic, and a policy checker, gives each step a defined input and output that can be logged, inspected, and tested on its own. This is the same principle that makes software engineering and human institutions trustworthy: separation of duties. We don't let the person who writes the check also approve it, and for the same reason a dedicated reviewer role, instructed only to find problems, catches errors that a single "do-it-all" prompt tends to rationalize away. Auditors can then point to exactly which stage failed, and engineers can improve that one component (swap a model, tighten an instruction, add a test) without destabilizing everything else. A monolithic prompt can sometimes perform impressively, but it is a black box. A role-based pipeline is a glass box, and safety and improvement depend on being able to see inside.

**Rebuttal:** The "glass box" is mostly an illusion. Logging each stage shows you *what* the retriever, drafter, and critic produced, but each of those roles is still an opaque model call. You've traded one black box for four, plus the seams between them. Many real failures live in those seams: the retriever surfaces a subtly wrong source, the drafter faithfully builds on it, and the critic, lacking the original context, approves a coherent-looking draft. Which stage "failed"? Each did its narrow job. That isn't clean diagnosis. It's distributed blame. The separation-of-duties analogy is also weaker than it sounds. Human auditors are independent people with different incentives and knowledge. A "critic" role is usually the same underlying model with the same blind spots and a different instruction. Its errors are correlated with the drafter's, so the independence is largely theatrical. Worse, it creates *false* assurance: a pipeline stamped "reviewed by critic" invites less human scrutiny than an output everyone knows came from a single pass. And "improve one component without destabilizing everything else" rarely holds. Downstream stages quietly adapt to upstream quirks, so swapping the retriever can break the drafter's assumptions in ways no unit test anticipated.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Splitting work into roles multiplies the surfaces where things go wrong, and each handoff is a lossy compression. Context the whole task needs (the user's intent, caveats, uncertainty, why a source looked shaky) gets summarized away as it passes between roles. This is precisely the information safety depends on. Each boundary is also a new injection point. Malicious text in a retrieved document can be passed downstream as trusted "research" to roles never designed to treat it as hostile. Meanwhile, a single capable model working with full context can surface its reasoning in one continuous trace and be evaluated end-to-end on the outcome that actually matters. To be fair, modular pipelines can genuinely help for some well-scoped, high-volume tasks. But the claim here is general: that splitting roles *makes* AI work safer and easier to audit. In practice it often adds complexity, cost, and correlated failure modes while producing an appearance of rigor. An appearance of rigor is arguably more dangerous than an honest black box, because it lowers our guard.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent's injection point actually argues for my side. In a single do-it-all prompt, a malicious retrieved document shares one context with the model's instructions *and* its tool permissions, so a successful injection can act directly. Role separation is the main structural defense here. The component that reads untrusted text can be denied tools entirely, and the component that can act never sees raw untrusted content. This is the "quarantined reader" pattern security researchers recommend precisely because monoliths can't enforce it. On lossy handoffs: a single long prompt loses context too, through attention dilution and instructions buried mid-context, but it does so invisibly. An explicit handoff forces designers to decide what must survive, such as intent, caveats, provenance and confidence, and to check that it did. And a monolith's "continuous reasoning trace" is not a glass box either, since stated reasoning is often not faithful to what actually drove the output.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Roles let you enforce *least privilege*, so each failure stays small. When one prompt holds every capability (search, write, send, approve), any error or manipulation has the full system's reach. When roles are split, each one gets only the permissions its job requires. The drafter cannot send. The retriever cannot write. The final action passes through a gate that can be a plain deterministic check rather than another model, such as a schema validator, a test that each citation matches its source, or a spending limit. That also answers the "correlated critic" worry. Not every seam needs to be an LLM, and the seams are exactly where you can insert checks that share none of the model's blind spots. I'll concede that pipelines can be over-engineered and that a "reviewed" stamp can breed complacency. But that is a governance failure that applies to any process. Bounding what each part is *allowed* to do, and placing independent checks between parts, is something only a split architecture makes possible.

**Rebuttal:** Least privilege is a genuinely good principle, but it doesn't require splitting the *AI work* into roles. You can wrap a single model in scoped tools, require human or deterministic approval before any irreversible action, and validate its outputs against schemas and spending limits. The gate sits between the model and the world, whatever happens upstream. So the safety gains my opponent describes come from *permissioning and gating*, not from decomposition itself. The quarantined-reader pattern is also leakier than presented. The privileged component still acts on whatever the reader passes it, so a poisoned summary ("the vendor's verified account is X") carries the attack across the boundary in clean-looking form. That is why serious defenses add capability and data-flow tracking rather than relying on role separation alone. And deterministic checks only catch what can be specified in advance. A test that each citation matches its source passes happily when the source itself is wrong, and the errors that matter most are usually semantic, not syntactic.

**My strongest remaining argument:** The "easier to improve" claim gets things backwards over any realistic time horizon. A pipeline freezes a human guess about how the task *should* be decomposed, and every stage is then tuned to local metrics: retrieval recall, critic flag rate, drafter fluency. These can each improve while the end result stagnates or gets worse, because what matters is the whole outcome, and Goodhart's law applies at every seam. In practice, the largest quality gains in AI systems have come from better models evaluated end-to-end. Elaborate scaffolding often becomes the bottleneck, encoding workarounds for weaknesses newer models no longer have, and it grows harder to remove because every component depends on the others. I'll grant that decomposition can earn its keep for stable, high-volume, well-specified tasks. But as a general rule, splitting roles mainly adds machinery to maintain and blame to distribute. The safer default is a capable model, tightly permissioned, judged on what it actually delivers.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent now locates the safety gains in "permissioning and gating," but a gate that approves actions independently of the model proposing them *is* a role split: proposer versus approver. That concedes the principle and disputes only the label. On improvement, Goodhart's law applies to a single end-to-end metric too, and pipelines are not exempt from end-to-end evaluation. You can and should test the whole system's outcomes *and* each stage. The difference is what happens when the score drops. An end-to-end eval tells you *that* something regressed; stage-level logs tell you *where*. As for scaffolding going stale, a discrete stage is the easiest kind to retire: delete it, rerun the end-to-end evals, and keep the change if nothing breaks. Workarounds buried in one sprawling prompt are far harder to find and remove. And the poisoned-summary attack is real, but typed handoffs, such as an allow-listed vendor ID or a schema with no free-text field, narrow what can cross a boundary in a way a monolith's single shared context never can.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Splitting roles makes the safety function itself *measurable*. If "check for errors and policy violations" is one instruction inside a do-it-all prompt, you cannot isolate how often that check works. Once the reviewer is its own role, you can feed it a labeled set of drafts with planted errors and measure its catch rate directly. You can also track that rate across model versions and compare alternatives. One alternative is a different model family, which directly reduces the correlated-blind-spot problem my opponent raised. This is what auditors, regulators and model-risk frameworks actually ask for: a documented control with a known, tested effectiveness and a named point where a human can intervene. I'll concede that decomposition has real costs and can be overdone. But "trust the capable model, judged on outcomes" offers no way to show *how* its safeguards perform, only that nothing bad has happened yet. A safeguard you can test in isolation is one you can audit and improve, and that is the core of this motion.

**Rebuttal:** Calling every check a "role split" stretches the motion until it can't lose. A schema validator or spending limit isn't a share of the *AI work*. It's a guardrail around it, and I've endorsed guardrails all along. The real dispute is whether dividing the reasoning itself across multiple model roles makes the system safer. On measurability, a reviewer's catch rate on *planted* errors measures how well it finds planted errors. Real errors are subtler, and in production the critic reviews drafts from a drafter whose blind spots it may share. The isolated score can look excellent while the in-pipeline catch rate is much lower, giving regulators a documented control with a number attached and a false sense of effectiveness. Nor is a monolith unmeasurable. You can red-team it end-to-end with seeded adversarial inputs and measure how often harmful or wrong outputs actually reach users, which is the only rate that ultimately matters. Using a different model family for review is a fair point and does reduce correlation, though it also adds a second vendor's failure modes. And stage logs tell you *where* only when the failure is local. The seam failures I described earlier still show every stage passing.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Stages don't just add their reliabilities, they *multiply* them, and the interactions can make outputs worse, not better. If four stages are each right 95% of the time and their errors are independent, the chain is right only about 81% of the time. Reviewer roles add a subtler problem: false positives. A critic told to find problems will find some, and a drafter told to fix them will "correct" text that was already right. Research on LLM self-correction has found that, without reliable external feedback, revision loops often turn correct answers into incorrect ones about as readily as the reverse. More roles also mean more prompts, more versions, and more interactions to test. The number of configurations grows combinatorially, and that tends to *reduce* real test coverage, whatever the per-stage dashboards show. I'll concede that well-specified, high-volume tasks with crisp intermediate outputs, like extraction followed by validation, benefit from decomposition. But the motion claims splitting roles generally *makes* AI safer and easier to audit. Often it simply moves the risk into handoffs and revision loops, while generating paperwork that looks like assurance.
For wins a close debate. Against landed real blows, but For tied its case more directly to the motion's claims about auditing and improvement and answered more of its opponent's arguments head-on.

output.reasoning: Both sides argued at a high level, but For engaged more directly with the motion's specific claims (safer, easier to audit, easier to improve) and more often turned its opponent's points to its own advantage. Against did land real blows. The 'four black boxes plus seams' critique, correlated critic errors, the risk of false assurance, and the poisoned-summary limit on quarantined readers were all sharp. Its final-round objection that deterministic guardrails are not really splits of the 'AI work' was a fair attempt to stop the motion from being stretched. However, For converted Against's prompt-injection argument into a case for role separation through quarantined readers and least privilege. It then answered the poisoned-summary reply with typed, allow-listed handoffs that Against never rebutted. For also gave a clear account of auditability: end-to-end evals show *that* a regression occurred, while stage logs show *where*. It made a strong case that an isolated reviewer role makes the safety function measurable, which a check buried inside one prompt cannot offer, and it addressed the correlation worry by suggesting a reviewer from a different model family. Against's late arguments were weaker. Against also repeatedly conceded that decomposition works for well-specified tasks and endorsed gating, which narrowed the dispute to ground where For's diagnostic and measurement arguments held up better. runs.name: plain-2
runs.topic: Splitting AI work into clear roles makes it safer and easier to audit and improve than one prompt doing it all

turns.content: When one prompt does everything (gathering facts, reasoning, drafting, and checking its own work), a failure shows up only as a bad final answer, and you can't tell which step went wrong. Splitting the work into clear roles, such as a retriever, a drafter, and an independent reviewer, turns that black box into a pipeline with inspectable seams. Each handoff produces an artifact you can log, test, and score on its own. If the output is wrong, you can see whether the retriever pulled the wrong document or the drafter misread the right one. That matters for safety, because a separate reviewer with a narrow mandate and no stake in the draft catches errors a model tends to rationalize when grading itself. It also matters for improvement, because you can fix or swap one weak component without retuning a sprawling prompt where every edit risks breaking something unrelated. This is the same reason we separate duties in accounting and code review: no single actor should both produce and approve the work. Role separation doesn't guarantee correctness, but it makes errors visible, attributable, and fixable, and that is what "auditable" means.

**Against:** My opponent's case rests on an analogy that doesn't hold. Separation of duties works in accounting because the clerk and the auditor are different people with different knowledge and incentives. A "retriever," "drafter," and "independent reviewer" are usually the same underlying model in different costumes, so they share the same blind spots. Their errors are correlated, not independent, and a reviewer that misreads a document the way the drafter did will approve the mistake. The "inspectable seams" are also where much of the damage happens. Each handoff compresses context, so the drafter never sees what the retriever discarded, and the reviewer never sees why the drafter chose its framing. Errors then emerge from the interaction itself, which is exactly what attribution struggles with. Studies of multi-agent failures repeatedly find many breakdowns in inter-agent misunderstanding and poorly specified handoffs rather than in any single role.

My strongest point is that splitting the work multiplies failure modes rather than isolating them. Every new role adds another prompt to maintain, another interface to break, and another path for prompt injection to travel from a retrieved document into downstream steps. It also creates a dangerous sense of assurance: a pipeline with a "reviewer" stage looks audited even when the review is a rubber stamp. A single well-structured prompt can still produce inspectable intermediate output: cited sources, explicit reasoning, a separate checklist section. It does this without the context loss and coordination overhead. Role separation can help in specific cases, especially when a stage is truly different, such as a deterministic validator or a human. But as a general rule, adding more parts gives you more logs, not more safety.

My opponent concedes the key point: stages help when they are truly different, such as a deterministic validator, a different model, or a human. But you can only insert those checks at a seam, so role separation is what makes diverse, uncorrelated review possible in the first place. The correlated-error worry also cuts the other way. Research on LLM self-correction (e.g., Huang et al., 2023) finds that models often fail to fix their own reasoning without external feedback. A reviewer that never sees the drafter's framing is less anchored to it, not more. Context loss at handoffs is real, but it is visible: you can log exactly what the retriever discarded and test it. In a single prompt, that same "discarding" happens silently inside attention. And the claim that one prompt can show its work through cited sources and explicit reasoning overlooks that self-reported reasoning is often unfaithful (Turpin et al., 2023). A retriever's output is a record of what was actually fetched, not the model's story about it. My new argument turns their injection point around: separation enables least privilege. In patterns like the "dual-LLM" design or CaMeL, the component that reads untrusted documents has no tools and no authority. The component that can act never sees raw untrusted text. A single do-everything prompt must hold both the poisoned input and the power to act in the same context, which is exactly the setup prompt injection exploits. More parts do mean more interfaces to maintain, but they are the only way to keep untrusted input and authority apart.

**Against:** My opponent's best examples prove my point. CaMeL and the dual-LLM pattern are not safe because work is split into roles. They are safe because a deterministic layer enforces capability limits and tracks which data is tainted. The quarantined model's output is treated as untrusted data and never read as instructions. Ordinary role splits lack that enforcement. A "researcher" agent summarizes a poisoned page and hands the summary to an "executor" agent with tools. That launders the injection: the attacker's text now arrives as trusted internal output. So the security comes from the enforcement mechanism, not the division of labor, and splitting without it can make things worse. The faithfulness argument also cuts both ways. A drafter's handoff note is just as much a self-report as a single prompt's reasoning. Meanwhile, a single agent's tool calls and retrieved documents are logged just as precisely as a separate retriever's. On Huang et al., the same paper found that multi-agent debate did no better than simple self-consistency once the number of responses was held equal. Extra LLM "reviewers" were not the external feedback that helped.

My strongest remaining argument is that the promised modular improvement is largely an illusion. Each stage gets its own metric, so teams optimize the retriever for recall and the drafter for fluency, and those local gains often fail to improve end-to-end quality. A retriever "improved" to return more documents can bury the one fact the drafter needed. You still have to evaluate the whole pipeline, and per-stage scores invite blame-shifting and Goodhart effects rather than real attribution. Fixed decompositions also lock in today's guess about how a task should be split. As models improve, they can often do the combined task better than the pipeline, but the scaffolding stays in place because every stage has its own tests and owners. Use real separation where it adds something different in kind: deterministic validators, capability boundaries, or human approval. As a general rule, though, carving one model's work into roles mostly adds overhead that looks like an audit trail.

**For:** My opponent's Goodhart worry argues for end-to-end evaluation, which I never opposed. It does not argue against stage artifacts. An end-to-end score tells you *that* the system failed, and stage outputs tell you *where*. Their own example shows this: if a retriever buries a key fact, you can only find that out by looking at the retriever's output and seeing that the fact was there and the drafter missed it. Without that artifact, the same failure is just "worse answers." Lock-in also cuts the other way. When evals show a newer model does the combined task better, a modular pipeline lets you merge two stages and measure the difference. A sprawling monolithic prompt is just as frozen, but nobody can say which instructions are still doing any work. On CaMeL, I agree that deterministic enforcement provides the security. But enforcement needs a boundary to act on. Taint tracking and capability limits only work if the system is already split into components with separate inputs and powers. Their "laundering" example describes a bad split, not an argument against splitting. My new point is that clear roles make risk-proportionate oversight possible. With defined stages, you can send only the risky step, such as an outbound payment or a published claim, to a human or a strict validator, and let low-stakes steps run freely. A single prompt forces a cruder choice: review everything, which humans won't sustain, or review nothing. Separation lets scarce human attention go where the stakes are. That is not overhead that looks like an audit trail. It is how audits actually get done.

**Against:** My opponent's risk-proportionate oversight doesn't require splitting the model's thinking into roles. It requires gating *actions*, and a single agent already exposes those as discrete tool calls. Most agent frameworks put the human approval on the tool call itself: "send_payment" or "publish" pauses for sign-off while reading and drafting run freely. The boundary sits at the tool layer, not between a "drafter" persona and a "reviewer" persona. The same applies to taint tracking and to their buried-fact example. A single agent's retrieval calls are logged verbatim, so you can see that the fact was fetched and then ignored without adding a separate retriever. Each time my opponent identifies something that actually helps, whether enforcement, diverse checkers, human gates, or logged artifacts, it turns out to live at tool and action boundaries that a single agent already has. Their own phrase, "a bad split," gives the game away. The topic claims that splitting makes systems safer, but splitting helps only when it coincides with these hard boundaries, and then the boundaries are doing the work.

My strongest remaining argument is cost. Multi-agent designs routinely use several times more tokens and latency. Anthropic, for example, reported that its multi-agent research system used roughly 15x the tokens of a chat interaction. Practitioner guides, including Anthropic's own "Building effective agents," advise starting with the simplest single-agent design and adding agents only when they demonstrably help. That budget has alternatives: a stronger model, more end-to-end evals, sampling multiple answers, or more human review at the action gates where it matters. So the honest rule is to put hard checks where stakes are high and keep the cognition unified. Carving one model into roles is sometimes worth it, but as a default it spends real money on the appearance of independence rather than on the checks that actually make systems safe and auditable.
Against wins. They showed, step by step, that each benefit For cited actually comes from hard boundaries a single agent already has, not from splitting the work into roles.

output.reasoning: Both sides argued well and cited evidence, but Against had the sharper logic and steadily narrowed what the motion could claim. For opened with a clear case: inspectable seams, an independent reviewer, the separation-of-duties analogy, and easier modular fixes. Against weakened that case early with the point about correlated errors, since the 'roles' are often the same model sharing the same blind spots, and noted that context loss at handoffs creates new failure modes. For's second round was its strongest, especially the least-privilege argument from the dual-LLM and CaMeL designs. Against then turned those same examples around: their security comes from deterministic enforcement and taint tracking, not from dividing the work, and naive splits can 'launder' an injection by passing attacker text along as trusted internal output. For's later replies (stage artifacts locate failures, enforcement needs a boundary, risk-proportionate oversight) were reasonable. But Against answered each one by showing it relies on tool and action boundaries a single agent already exposes: logged retrieval calls, approval gates on actions like payments, and capability limits. Against also seized on For's phrase 'a bad split,' arguing that splitting helps only when it coincides with those hard boundaries, which then do the real work. This undercut the motion's general claim that role separation itself makes systems safer and more auditable. Against's cost argument was somewhat loose: the 15x token figure compares a multi-agent system with ordinary chat, not with a single agent doing the same task. It was also a final-round point For could not answer, so it counted for little. Even so, Against's core distinction between role decomposition and enforcement boundaries went largely unrefuted. For never fully explained why splitting cognition into personas, as opposed to gating actions, adds safety beyond what those boundaries already provide.

runs.topic: Splitting AI work into clear roles makes it safer and easier to audit and improve than one prompt doing it all

turns.content: **Opening argument:** When one prompt does everything (research, reasoning, writing, checking its own work), every failure becomes a mystery. If the output is wrong, was the retrieval bad, the reasoning flawed, or the formatting garbled? You can't tell, because it all happened inside one opaque pass. Splitting the work into clear roles, like a retriever, a drafter, and a reviewer, creates natural checkpoints where each intermediate output can be logged, inspected, and tested on its own. That's the same principle that makes software modular and organizations use separation of duties: an accountant doesn't audit their own books, because independent checks catch errors that self-review misses. Role separation also limits blast radius. A component that only summarizes documents doesn't need permission to send emails or execute code, so a prompt injection or hallucination in one stage can't freely cascade into harmful actions. Improvement gets easier too. When you can measure each role separately, you can fix the weak link (swap in a better retriever, tighten the reviewer's rubric) without re-engineering the whole system and hoping nothing else breaks. To be fair, splitting adds coordination overhead. But for anything where safety and accountability matter, being able to see where something went wrong and fix exactly that part is worth far more than the convenience of a single monolithic prompt.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent's case depends on the assumption that splitting work creates *independent* checks, and that assumption is weaker than it sounds. The accountant analogy works because the auditor is a different person with different incentives and knowledge. An AI "reviewer" is usually the same underlying model, or a close cousin, with the same training and the same blind spots. Its errors are correlated with the drafter's, so it tends to approve exactly the mistakes it would have made itself. That gives you the *appearance* of independent review without the substance, which arguably makes oversight worse by building false confidence.

The blast-radius point also confuses two separate things. Permission scoping is a property of tool access, not of role-splitting: you can deny a single agent email or code-execution rights just as easily. Meanwhile, pipelines create new attack surfaces. Injected text in a retrieved document gets passed downstream as a "trusted" intermediate output, effectively laundered by the stage before it. And checkpoints only tell you something if the interfaces between stages are well defined. In practice, many failures happen *at* the handoffs, which is precisely where a split architecture is most opaque.

**My strongest argument:** Every handoff is lossy, and losses compound. When a retriever passes a summary to a drafter, which passes a draft to a reviewer, each stage discards context the next one may need: the nuance in the source, the reason a caveat mattered, the user's original intent. Errors multiply too. Five stages that are each 95% reliable yield roughly 77% end-to-end reliability. A single capable model holding the full context can notice that a retrieved fact contradicts the user's question, or that a caveat must survive into the final answer, because it never lost sight of the whole problem. Auditability doesn't require fragmentation either. One model with full reasoning traces, logged tool calls, and an external evaluation harness can be inspected step by step without introducing new failure points. Role-splitting has real uses, but presenting it as inherently "safer and easier to audit" ignores that it often trades visible, holistic reasoning for brittle seams where meaning and accountability slip through the cracks.

**Rebuttal and closing argument:** The compounding-error math cuts against my opponent, not for them. A single prompt doing retrieval, reasoning, drafting, and checking faces the same chain of subtasks. Its failures still multiply; you just can't see which link broke or measure each one's reliability. Splitting doesn't create those failure points. It exposes them, so a 95% stage can be raised to 99% instead of hidden in an aggregate score. Lossy handoffs are a design choice, not an inevitability: pipelines can pass the original query and source passages forward alongside summaries, and when context is dropped, it's dropped in a logged artifact you can inspect. A monolith "losing sight" of a caveat leaves no trace at all. That points to the deepest flaw in the "just use reasoning traces" alternative. Research on chain-of-thought faithfulness shows a model's stated reasoning can diverge from what actually drove its answer, so a trace can be a plausible story rather than a record. In a pipeline, the intermediate outputs *are* the causal inputs to the next stage, so auditing them audits what actually happened. On correlated reviewers, I grant the point when the same model rubber-stamps itself. But role separation is what lets you break that correlation: you can use a different model for review, add deterministic validators like citation checks or schema checks, or give the reviewer a narrow rubric instead of the drafter's framing. Those options barely exist when one prompt grades its own homework. Splitting doesn't guarantee safety, but it gives you real, causally grounded checkpoints where failures can be found, measured, and fixed. A single prompt asks you to trust a story about what happened inside it.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent's best point is that pipeline artifacts are causal while reasoning traces may be unfaithful. But that advantage is smaller than claimed. A logged handoff shows *what* a stage produced, not *why*. Each stage is still an opaque model pass with the same faithfulness problem, now repeated at every step. And the causal checkpoints they credit to role-splitting are available to a single agent too. Its retrieval results, tool calls, and outputs are logged artifacts that actually drove the answer. The remedies they offer for correlated review (deterministic citation checks, schema validators, a different grading model) are external evaluation layers. They can wrap a single model's output just as easily. They don't require carving the work itself into roles.

I also disagree that splitting merely "exposes" failure points the monolith already had. A model holding full context can catch and correct its own mid-course errors. A pipeline adds failures that didn't exist before: misread handoffs, format mismatches, and lost intent. Passing everything forward fixes lossy handoffs, but then each stage carries the full context, and the separation starts to dissolve.

**My strongest remaining argument:** "Easier to improve" is the weakest part of the motion, because tuning stages locally can make the whole system worse. Optimize the retriever for recall and it floods the drafter with noise. Tighten the reviewer's rubric and the drafter learns to write for the rubric rather than the user. Components quietly adapt to each other's quirks, so "swap in a better retriever" often breaks assumptions nobody wrote down. Split systems also spread accountability thin. When the final answer is wrong, every stage can show it met its local spec, and the failure belongs to no one. Meanwhile, a pipeline locks in today's guess about how the task should be divided, while end-to-end systems keep improving as models do. Role-splitting is a useful tool for specific risks. But it is not *inherently* safer, easier to audit, or easier to improve, and treating it as a default trades one honest black box for many smaller ones plus the gaps between them.

**Rebuttal and final argument:** My opponent's toolkit concedes the motion. A single agent whose retrieval is logged separately, whose output is checked by citation and schema validators, and whose work is graded by a different model *is* a role-split system: retrieval, generation, and verification are distinct parts with their own interfaces. The remaining dispute is how far to split, not whether splitting helps. On local optimization, Goodhart's law applies at least as much to the monolith. Edit a mega-prompt to fix one behavior and another quietly breaks, with no way to tell which instruction caused it. Split systems still need end-to-end evaluation. Stage metrics are for diagnosis, not a replacement. And "every stage met its spec, yet the answer was wrong" is not lost accountability. It is a finding: the failure sits in a specific interface or spec, which you can fix. "The model got it wrong" points nowhere. Lock-in runs the other way too. Modular stages can be merged as models improve, while a monolith's implicit structure can't be selectively upgraded. My strongest remaining argument is that the most important safety control is a human or deterministic gate before irreversible actions, and gates need boundaries. You can require approval between "draft the wire transfer" and "execute it" only if those are separate steps with an inspectable handoff. One prompt that plans and acts in a single pass gives you nowhere to stand. Splitting isn't free or automatic, but it is what makes those checkpoints possible.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent now counts every log, validator, and permission check as "role-splitting." But that stretches the motion until it is trivially true. The motion contrasts splitting *AI work* into roles with *one prompt doing it all*. A schema validator, a citation checker, or an approval prompt is not an AI role. Each role can also be given only the permissions it needs, so a summarizer never holds the tool that sends emails or executes code. And because each role has a narrow, testable job, you can build targeted evaluations, swap in a better model for one step, and measure the improvement directly. Clear roles turn an opaque process into an engineered one.
